opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting open questions right now. When we look at where these models are today, they've gotten remarkably good at solving hard, well-posed problems, things like competition math, where there's a clear statement, a known kind of answer, and you can check your work. That's a big milestone, but it's a different skill from what a working mathematician does day to day.

A lot of real mathematical progress isn't about solving a problem someone handed you. It's about figuring out which questions are worth asking, noticing that two seemingly unrelated areas share some hidden structure, or inventing the right definition so that a messy problem suddenly becomes clean. Some of the biggest advances in history came less from clever tricks than from new frameworks, a new way of seeing things. That kind of taste and judgment is harder to train for, partly because it's harder to verify. With an olympiad problem you know when you're right. With "is this a fruitful new concept?" the feedback loop can take years, or even decades.

That said, I'm fairly optimistic. The reasoning abilities we're seeing aren't narrow. The models are learning to explore, to try ideas, to backtrack, to stay with a problem for a long time. As they get better at sustained thinking over hours or days instead of minutes, I think we'll see them first become genuinely useful collaborators: proving lemmas, checking cases, suggesting approaches a human might not have considered. From there, it's not a huge conceptual leap to models proposing their own conjectures and building out new theory.

I don't think it'll be a single moment where an AI suddenly invents a new field. It'll probably be more gradual. More and more of the creative work gets shared between people and models, until at some point we look back and realize a meaningful share of the new ideas came from the model. And honestly, I think mathematicians will be some of the people most excited about that, because there are so many questions we'd love answers to and nowhere near enough time to explore them all.

r001.rationale: It contrasts models’ success on well-posed problems with the harder work of choosing questions, finding hidden structure, and inventing useful definitions or frameworks.

r002.rationale: It mentions sustained thinking over hours or days, but does not say the duration models can work independently roughly doubles every few months.

r003.rationale: It says evaluating whether a new concept is fruitful can take years or decades; it does not frame inventing new ways of doing mathematics itself as taking that long.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, partly because I came up through competition math, and the thing competition math teaches you is that there's a huge difference between solving a problem someone hands you and figuring out what the right problem even is.

So let me separate two things. The first is: can these models produce new, correct mathematics? And I think the answer there is already yes, in a narrow sense. When we were working on the IMO gold result, one of the things that struck me was not just that the model got the answers, but that some of the proofs took routes I hadn't seen before. They weren't retrievals of a known argument. The model was doing genuine search over proof space and landing on something that worked. If you scale that same capability up to open problems, you get a model that can, with enough compute and verification, grind out results that no human has written down. That's new mathematics in the literal sense, and I'd expect a steady stream of that over the next few years, especially in areas where checking a proof is mechanical.

The second question is harder, and it's the one you actually asked about: new forms of mathematics. Not a new theorem, but a new framework. Something like Grothendieck inventing schemes, or the way category theory reorganized how people think. That's a different kind of act. It's less about proving and more about taste, about noticing that a bunch of disparate things are secretly the same thing, and then having the conviction to build the language for it before you can prove it pays off.

My honest view is that I don't think there's a hard barrier there, but I think it's further out than people expect, and for a slightly subtle reason. The reinforcement learning loop that makes reasoning models good at proofs works because there's a clean reward signal: the proof is right or it's wrong. Inventing a new abstraction doesn't come with that. The reward for a good definition shows up years later, when it turns out to make a hundred other problems tractable. So the model has to learn to value things that don't cash out immediately, and we're still early on training for that kind of long-horizon judgment.

What gives me optimism is that the ingredients are starting to show up. We're seeing models that will spontaneously introduce a lemma or a helper construction mid-proof, which is a small-scale version of the same instinct. And once you have a model that can run thousands of parallel explorations, it can afford to try abstractions that a human mathematician would never gamble a decade on. Some of those are going to be bad, and some of them are going to be things we look at and say, huh, I never would have thought to carve it up that way.

So I'd put it like this: new theorems, soon and in volume. New definitions that humans adopt, within the decade, probably first in computational or combinatorial areas. Genuinely new fields of mathematics that reshape how we think, I'm less certain, but I've stopped betting against these systems on timelines. Every time I've done that I've been wrong in the same direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts models’ ability to find new proofs and solve problems with the harder task of inventing frameworks, which it says requires taste and long-horizon judgment.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives no claim that the human-equivalent duration of independent mathematical work doubles every few months.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes new frameworks as taking longer to emerge and says a useful abstraction may take years to pay off; it also refers to a human mathematician gambling a decade on an abstraction.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really exciting possibility. There’s a difference between solving a problem within an existing mathematical framework and inventing a new framework that makes a whole class of problems easier to understand. The second one is a much more open-ended task. You have to decide what definitions are useful, which questions are worth asking, and whether an idea connects things that previously looked unrelated.

Reasoning models could potentially help with that by exploring examples, proposing definitions, and working through their consequences. But producing something new isn’t enough—you can invent arbitrary mathematical structures all day. The hard part is finding something that’s useful or illuminating.

So I’m optimistic, but I’d distinguish being very good at answering mathematical questions from being very good at choosing the questions and developing the language to answer them. I’d expect progress to involve a lot of interaction between mathematicians and models, with each helping the other recognize which ideas are worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes solving within existing frameworks from inventing frameworks, but does not clearly describe current reasoning models as strong at finding solutions and weak at inventing new theories.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate that the duration of mathematical work models can perform independently doubles every few months.

r003.rationale: It calls invention open-ended and difficult, but does not frame it as requiring years or decades.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really exciting possibility. There’s a spectrum between solving a problem within an existing mathematical framework and inventing a new framework that makes a whole class of problems easier to understand. The second is harder to evaluate, because a new definition isn’t useful just because it’s new. It has to reveal something.

Reasoning models give us a way to explore that: can a model notice a pattern, formulate a conjecture, and develop the concepts needed to explain it? Checking a proof gives you a fairly concrete signal. Figuring out whether a new concept is fruitful takes longer—you need to see what other mathematics it enables.

So I’d be excited to see models participate in that whole process, alongside mathematicians. Not just answering questions we already know how to ask, but helping us discover which questions are worth asking.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts solving within an existing framework with inventing one, but does not say current reasoning models are strong at the former and weak at the latter.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate that models’ independent mathematical work duration roughly doubles every few months.

r003.rationale: It says evaluating a fruitful new concept takes longer, but does not frame inventing new mathematics as requiring years or decades.
